title: White pepper and loess
subtitle: Why Grüner tastes as it does
objectives: Explain the role of loess soils

steps.title: Rotundone
steps.body: Grüner's white pepper note comes from rotundone, the same compound that gives Syrah its black pepper aroma and is found in peppercorns. It forms in the skins, especially in cooler sites and years. Like in Syrah, about one in five people can't smell it at all.

steps.title: Loess
steps.body: Grüner grows best on loess, a fine, wind-blown, yellowish silt deposited after the last ice age. Loess is deep, holds water and warms easily, giving full-bodied, rounder Grüner. In the Wachau and Kamptal, loess terraces sit beside primary rock, gneiss and granite, which give leaner, more mineral Grüner, often used for Riesling.

steps.prompt: The compound that gives Grüner its white pepper note is ____.
steps.explanation: Rotundone, also found in Syrah and peppercorns.

steps.title: Light to powerful
steps.body: Light Grüner, like many Weinviertel and Steinfeder wines, is crisp, peppery and best young. Powerful Grüner, like Wachau Smaragd or Kamptal Reserve from loess, is rich, with stone fruit, spice and a creamy texture, and can age 10 to 20 years, gaining honey and toast.

steps.explanation: Primary rock, not loess, gives leaner wines.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rotundone gives Grüner its white pepper
Loess gives full, round Grüner; rock gives mineral wines
Styles range from light to powerful and age-worthy
